extracted.subtask_description: A short news report documenting an instance of alleged journalistic plagiarism, the specific copied passages, and the editorial response (suspension and apologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unattributed copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not take 'substantial' portions of another publication's reporting without attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states the reporter "took 'substantial' portions of two recent articles from another publication without attribution." This implies that any reuse of material from another outlet requires clear attribution and that substantial verbatim or closely paraphrased passages are unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of copied material factors into severity
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent/quantity of copied text is a key factor in evaluating misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story cites specific examples — two paragraphs taken from one Arizona Republic story and 10 paragraphs taken from another — and labels those as 'substantial,' indicating that even a small number of paragraphs can be treated seriously. Editors assess the amount and significance of the copied material when determining wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consequences for plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications may impose disciplinary action (e.g., suspension) when a reporter is found to have plagiarized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Washington Post suspended Sari Horwitz after editors concluded she copied material without attribution. This exemplifies that formal sanctions (suspension, reprimand, termination) are possible outcomes following editorial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to apologize and correct the record
rubrics_metrics.description: When plagiarism is discovered, both the journalist and the publication are expected to issue apologies or corrections to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that "The Post and Horwitz each issued separate apologies to their readers," indicating that public apology and acknowledgement are standard remedial steps following confirmed misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: No immunity for established or award-winning journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Past recognition or awards do not exempt a journalist from accountability for ethical breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece mentions Horwitz's Pulitzer Prize (2002) yet reports she was still suspended, illustrating that professional acclaim does not shield individuals from consequences for plagiarism.
